course.title: Camday – Cambridge Lower Secondary Mathematics — Stage 7

unit.title: Interpreting and Discussing Results
unit.blurb: Two-way tables, dual and compound bar charts, pie charts and waffle diagrams, infographics, choosing a chart, and the mode, median, mean and range.
unit.subject: maths

O2.t: Draw and interpret dual and compound bar charts.

O3.t: Interpret pie charts and waffle diagrams as parts of a whole.

O4.t: Read information from infographics and comment on how they present data.

O5.t: Choose a suitable way to represent a set of data.

O6.t: Find the mode, median, mean and range and use them to compare data.

p: A canteen records lunches for one day: **Year 7 and Year 8 students** choose **pasta, rice or salad**. 64 students ate lunch.
How could you record both the year and the choice in one table, so you can answer 'How many Year 8s chose salad?' Think about it before you read on.
The total of a row is the sum of the numbers in it.
A **two-way table** shows data sorted in two ways at once – here by year (rows) and lunch (columns). The **totals** row and column help check and fill gaps.
p2: 9 Year 8s chose salad. 26 students chose pasta. Every row and column adds up, and both sets of totals give 64.

p: Use the totals: a missing number = total − the others in that row (or column).
Then check the grand total both ways (down the totals column and along the totals row).

qq.prompt: Using the lunch table, how many Year 7 students chose rice?

lesson.t: How do I complete and use a two-way table?
p: Step 1: Read the labels: what do the rows and columns show?
Step 2: Fill a gap where only one value is missing in a row or column.
Step 3: Keep going until the table is complete; check the grand total both ways.
Step 4: Answer the question using the right row and column (or a total).

p: A class records hours of screen time at the weekend for **boys and girls**: Saturday boys 4, girls 3; Sunday boys 5, girls 4.
How could one chart show both days AND both groups clearly? Think about it before you read on.
Bar heights show frequencies; read the scale carefully.

qq.prompt: A bar reaches halfway between 10 and 20 on the scale. Value?

p: A **dual bar chart** puts two bars side by side for each category, in two colours with a key. It is good for **comparing two groups** category by category.
p2: Boys had more screen time than girls on both days; both groups had more on Sunday.

p: A **compound (stacked) bar chart** stacks the groups on top of each other in one bar. The **total** height shows the whole; each section shows a part.
p2: Use a compound bar chart when the **totals** matter as well as the parts.

qq.prompt: From the dual bar chart: how many more hours did boys have than girls on Sunday?

lesson.t: How do I draw and read dual and compound bar charts?
p: Step 1: Choose: dual (compare groups) or compound (show totals and parts).
Step 2: Draw axes with a clear scale, labels and a key.
Step 3: Dual: two bars side by side per category. Compound: stack the parts; the top of the bar is the total.
Step 4: When reading a compound bar, subtract to find a section: top − bottom.

p: A survey of **120 students** shows how they travel to school: half walk, a quarter take the bus, and the rest come by car or bike.
How could a picture show these parts of the whole at a glance? Try it before you read on.
A full turn is 360°: half is 180°, a quarter is 90°.
A **pie chart** is a circle split into sectors. Each sector's angle is in proportion to its frequency: angle = frequency ÷ total × 360°.
p2: Pie charts show **proportions** of the whole, not the actual numbers – unless you know the total.

p: A **waffle diagram** is a 10 × 10 grid: each square is **1%**. Shading 45 squares shows 45%.
p2: Waffles make percentages easy to count.

qq.prompt: 30 out of 90 students chose music. What angle on a pie chart?

lesson.t: How do I read and draw pie charts?
p: Step 1: Find the total frequency.
Step 2: Angle for each group = frequency ÷ total × 360° (or degrees per item = 360 ÷ total).
Step 3: Draw with a protractor; check the angles add to 360°.
Step 4: To read: frequency = angle ÷ 360 × total.

lesson.a: School A – even though its sector is smaller

lesson.why: Sector size shows the proportion, not the number. A: 1/2 × 20 = 10; B: 1/4 × 40 = 10 – the same number.

p: You can't compare actual numbers in two pie charts without knowing their totals.

p: An **infographic** combines pictures, icons, short text and simple charts to present information quickly. Common parts:
Infographics are designed to grab attention, so check:
• **Scale**: icons should be the same size; making one picture taller AND wider exaggerates the difference.
• **Source and sample**: who collected the data and how many?
• **Units and totals**: '50% more' than what?
A bath drawn 2.5 times as tall and 2.5 times as wide as a shower looks about 6 times bigger, even though it is only 2.5 times the water.

p: Two basketball players' points in their last 5 games: **Ana: 12, 15, 11, 14, 13** and **Bo: 4, 25, 9, 22, 5**.
Who scores more on average? Who is more consistent? Try it before you read on.
Write data in order, smallest first: 12, 15, 11, 14, 13 → 11, 12, 13, 14, 15.

head: Average
How to find it
Ana
Bo
rows: the middle value when in order

p2: Both players have a mean of 13 points.

p: The **range** = largest − smallest. It measures **consistency**: a smaller range means more consistent.
Ana: 15 − 11 = **4**. Bo: 25 − 4 = **21**. Same mean, but Ana is far more consistent.
To compare two sets of data, compare an **average** (which is bigger?) AND the **range** (which is more spread out?), and write a sentence in context.

errs.fb: Divide the total by how many values.

lesson.t: How do I compare two sets of data?
p: Step 1: Find an average for each (mean, median or mode).
Step 2: Find the range for each.
Step 3: Compare: which average is higher? which range is smaller?
Step 4: Write two sentences in context, e.g. 'On average A scored more; B was more consistent.'
